speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: I will start with the first part on reducing the emissions of hydrofluorocarbon, or HFC, refrigerants from RAC equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: In recent months, the world witnessed the devastating impacts of climate change, from the unprecedented heatwaves in North America, to the terrifying floods in Europe and China.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC, in its latest report, warned of catastrophic impacts from climate change unless the world takes urgent action to curb greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and I am heartened by the strong support given by this House earlier this year in acknowledging climate change as a global emergency and a threat to mankind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Every tonne of GHG reduced can and will lead to tangible improvements to our environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Singapore will play our part to meet ambitious GHG emissions reduction targets.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These are set out under the 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution and our Long-Term Low-Emissions Development Strategy under the Paris Agreement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Earlier this year, we launched the Singapore Green Plan 2030, our national roadmap towards sustainable development.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We will review our plans and continue to raise our climate ambitions as low-emission technologies become available to achieve net zero emissions as soon as viable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: One significant contributor to GHG emissions is the use of RAC equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Cooling is essential in our hot and humid climate but it is energy-intensive and generates carbon emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: RAC equipment also use HFCs as refrigerants and emit HFCs into the atmosphere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These are potent GHGs which trap more heat than carbon dioxide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This is why MSE announced a comprehensive package of measures at the Committee of Supply debates last year to reduce HFC emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: First, to shift the market towards climate-friendly RAC equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This addresses the root cause, by avoiding the use of certain classes of HFC refrigerants that have the most adverse impact on the climate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Second, to raise the industry’s competency in handling HFC refrigerants during the installation, maintenance and decommissioning of the RAC equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Third, to mandate the recovery of spent HFC refrigerants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: HFCs from discarded RAC equipment will have to be collected and treated for reuse or destroyed, instead of being vented into the atmosphere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: First, we will phase out RAC equipment using refrigerants with high Global Warming Potential, or GWP in short, where climate-friendly alternatives are already available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: GWP is a measure of the warming effect of a gas relative to carbon dioxide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: For example, the typical refrigerant used in chillers, R134a, has a GWP of 1,300.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: In comparison, carbon dioxide has a GWP of one.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The higher the GWP, the more heat the refrigerant will trap.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Climate-friendly alternatives for such equipment are widely available.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: They are typically more energy-efficient and users can enjoy energy cost savings, too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: For households, there is no cost difference in switching to climate-friendly refrigerators and air-conditioners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: In our industry consultations, most suppliers and importers of RAC equipment have affirmed that they are able to supply climate-friendly models.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Countries in the EU, as well as the US and Japan, have implemented similar measures to curb HFC emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Major exporters of RAC equipment, such as the US and China, are also shifting towards more climate-friendly refrigerants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These measures will be effected through sections 40B to 40D, which allow the Minister to prescribe the above RAC equipment as goods to be regulated and the requirements that they have to satisfy to be supplied in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Sections 40E to 40G lay out the requirements for suppliers to register themselves and their RAC equipment with NEA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This allows NEA to regularly review the standards of these RAC equipment and ensure that the equipment sold in Singapore is climate friendly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Second, to raise the industry’s competency in handling refrigerants, we will regulate companies that carry out regulated GHG works.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: GHG works involve the use or handling of any GHG, such as the installation, maintenance and decommissioning of RAC equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Companies that carry out any regulated GHG works will be required to establish and maintain policies, procedures and processes to carry out the regulated GHG works safely to minimise emissions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: They must keep accurate records of those regulated GHG works and provide the records to NEA upon request.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Regulated companies must provide their employees with adequate and properly maintained equipment to carry out the regulated GHG works and deploy at least one competent technician to supervise or carry out such works.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: To be certified as competent, technicians must attend a training and certification programme that will equip them with the necessary skills to minimise HFC emissions when carrying out regulated GHG works.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The training programmes will uplift the capabilities of technicians and harmonise HFC handling practices across the industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Competent technicians will need to comply with the policies, procedures and processes set out by their respective companies as well as prescribed statutory requirements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Companies handling household refrigerators and air-conditioners will not have these requirements imposed on them but are encouraged to certify their technicians.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Sections 40K to 40P will allow the Minister to prescribe the classes, descriptions or types of GHG works to be regulated and the requirements for companies carrying out such regulated GHG works, including registering themselves with NEA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The responsibilities of competent technicians are set out in section 40Q.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Third, we will introduce measures to minimise the venting of spent refrigerants into the atmosphere.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Bill will introduce a related amendment to the definition of "industrial waste" in section 2 of the Environmental Public Health Act to classify spent refrigerants as "industrial waste".

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: With this change, spent refrigerants recovered during RAC equipment servicing and disposal must be sent for proper treatment by licensed toxic industrial waste collectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Director-General will be empowered to administer and enforce the new Part 10A and to conduct the necessary inspections, tests and surveys to make sure that the requirements in the Part are complied with.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These powers are set out in sections 40S to 40W.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The Director-General will also be given the power to grant waivers from specific requirements, as set out under section 40Y.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These waivers will be considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The key offences set out in Part 10A include carrying out regulated activities without registering with NEA, supplying non-compliant GHG goods that are regulated goods, failing to meet stipulated requirements, failing to provide records relating to regulated goods or regulated GHG works and falsifying data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The penalties for these offences are pegged to similar offences under the Energy Conservation Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: An appeal process, detailed in sections 40J and 40R, will also be put in place with regard to certain decisions of the Director-General concerning matters, such as registration.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Reconsideration can be sought from the Director-General in the first instance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We can expect further abatement beyond 2030 when the current stock of less climate-friendly equipment is completely phased out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Singapore is a dense, highly urbanised and vibrant city, and some amount of noise is normal and inevitable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This includes noise from construction projects which are needed to build our homes, MRT lines and our healthcare facilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Over the years, we have introduced a suite of measures to manage construction noise.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: First, NEA stipulates maximum permissible noise limits for construction sites, taking reference from the World Health Organization’s guidelines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Construction sites within 150 metres from residential buildings and noise-sensitive premises, such as hospitals, are subject to more stringent noise limits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Contractors must install noise meters at the nearest affected premises and monitor the noise levels regularly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Second, in 2011, we implemented the no-work rule to provide residents with greater quiet on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: No work is allowed on these days at construction sites located within 150 metres of any hospital, home for the aged sick or residential building, though NEA may grant permits for quieter forms of work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: These include using quieter piling and hacking equipment, and installing noise barriers and enclosures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: While most contractors comply with noise management measures, there is a small group of contractors that has continued to violate the no-work rule.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: From 2016 to 2020, NEA prosecuted an average of 3% of construction sites, or around 150 sites, for first-time violation of the no-work rule each year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: Twenty-two percent of this group would go on to repeat the offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: When complaints on construction noise are received, NEA strives to respond swiftly to address the noise disturbance, especially on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: However, there are limitations to the current enforcement approach, as violations of the no-work rule can only be confirmed through physical site inspections by NEA officers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This is resource-intensive and not always effective, as the breach of the no-work rule could have stopped by the time NEA officers reach the construction site.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This is where technology can make a difference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: It empowers the Director-General to require the owner or occupier of a construction site who has contravened the no-work rule to install, maintain and operate an electronic video surveillance system at their own cost.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: This includes visual monitoring devices, such as closed-circuit television cameras.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We recognise that the construction sector is facing significant challenges during this pandemic, such as a manpower crunch arising from border control measures and higher costs of construction materials.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The new requirement will not affect the vast majority of compliant construction sites.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: It will only be imposed on the small number of construction sites that have violated the no-work rule and it is meant to deter further violations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The first part of the Bill will ensure that we meet Singapore’s cooling needs in a responsible manner, by using climate-friendly RAC equipment and building up the industry’s competency in handling these equipment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: The second part of the Bill will maintain a conducive living environment by strengthening enforcement on offenders of the no-work rule.

speaker: The Minister of State for Sustainability and the Environment (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment)
text: We will continue to work with the industry and other key stakeholders to regularly review our approach of managing construction noise, taking into account public feedback, international best practices and our local context.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Residents will be happy to hear that the Bill empowers NEA to more effectively ensure that construction sites remain quiet on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans should also be happy that the Bill empowers the Government to better mitigate climate change, given that Singapore is getting warmer much more quickly than the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point relates to our efforts to reduce HFCs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that these contribute to about half of the emissions and the question is: what about the other half?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When can we expect to address emissions from the remaining types of equipment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond using the stick, can we offer more carrots, especially in terms of the remaining types of equipment that are currently not regulated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we increase grants for businesses to encourage adoption of cooling equipment with lower global warming potential?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All these while we work on stricter regulations and an eventual ban on the remaining types of equipment which are currently not regulated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification is about the requirements for becoming a competent person for carrying out greenhouse gas work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Training and certification are important to upskill our workforce, improve quality of services and reduce emissions by preventing leakage of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, training and tests are often conducted in English, which not all of our existing technicians may be fluent in, causing them to be disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important that certification is accessible and fair so that we improve our workforce rather than cause some to be excluded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the intended format of training and tests, whether they will be multilingual and what other measures will be implemented to support our existing technicians in getting certified?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and final clarification relates to the control of construction noise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the post-COVID-19 world, more activities are taking place from the home, such as remote learning and working.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will give families more quiet time to rest and recover over the weekend.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share what other measures do agencies have in place to manage construction noise in residential areas?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The EPMA is the primary regulation for the environmental control of pollution and waste, including for hazardous substances in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What I believe to be noteworthy in this amendment Bill is clause 3 of the Bill which inserts a new Part 10A, comprising new sections 40A to 40Y, relating to the control of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, anthropogenic greenhouse gases, with their far-ranging environmental and health effects, are just about the most hazardous substances nations around the world have to grapple with today.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bill goes into significant technical detail about the regulation, monitoring, prohibition and enforcement against a subset of greenhouse gas goods and related activities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, I believe it is also crucial that we do not lose sight of the big picture in terms of the urgent and bold actions that the Government, as well as all other governments around the world, have to undertake to curb greenhouse gas emissions adequately, in order to deal with the existential threat of climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today's debate is thus timely in the context of the recent August release of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change or IPCC's sixth Assessment Report or AR6 and as nations around the world prepare for COP26 at the 26th UN Climate Change conference coming up in November this year.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the recently published IPCC report "a code red for humanity", as it confirmed that we are observing unprecedented changes in the Earth’s climate "in every region and across the climate ecosystem".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It makes clear that the world faces a frightening future, even if – and that is a big "if" – the global economy is decarbonised rapidly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would thus like to spend some time sharing more about the key implications of this report and also what we should do in light of these implications, especially since this could have serious repercussions on a coastal island nation that is our home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2019, atmospheric Carbon Dioxide (CO2) concentrations were higher than at any time in at least two million years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Across all scenarios considered by the IPCC, global temperatures will continue to increase until at least the mid-century.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we are now expected to reach this 1.5 degree celsius tipping point earlier than expected.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unless immediate, rapid and large-scale action is taken to reduce emissions, the average global temperature is likely to reach or cross the 1.5 degree celsius warming threshold within 20 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, however, some climate changes are already locked in.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hot extremes have become more frequent and more intense across most land regions since the 1950s, while cold extremes have become less frequent and less severe.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With global emissions currently at a little more than 40 GtCO2 a year and if continued, the budget would be exhausted in a mere 12 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is certainly not spared from the effects of a higher global temperature.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even in a 1.5 degree celsius warmer world, there will an increase in the number of unprecedented weather events with disasters to become more frequent and intense.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Should emissions not come down to net zero by around 2050, there will be even more punishing heatwaves, severe coastal flooding events and bouts of heavier rain.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it is, Singapore has already seen record rainfalls in January, April and August.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The recent memory of flash floods in August this year is a very sombre reminder of how things are no longer the way it used to be.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What does this mean for daily life in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Local temperatures are 1.8 degree celsius higher than they were in 1948, as indicated in the MET Service database.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, global temperatures have warmed by about 1.1 degree celsius from pre-industrial times, which ended around 1850.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The IPCC has identified Southeast Asia as a region experiencing severe heat waves, which used to occur once every 50 years but have become five times more frequent.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Tropical cyclones are also getting stronger, severe droughts are happening 1.7 times as often and fire seasons are increasing in duration and intensity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Southeast Asia would likely experience this, resulting in flash floods if the ground is covered with concrete and if drainage systems are overwhelmed, as in Singapore’s case recently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, sea level rises in Asia, especially critical to low-lying coastal regions like Singapore, are projected to increase faster than global average, alongside coastal area loss and shoreline retreat.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While there has been much focus on CO2, the IPCC also assessed the possibility of actively targeting and removing methane as part of the pathway to limiting warming.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I had earlier filed a Parliamentary Question on whether the Government has conducted a study to assess the amount of external methane emissions associated with natural gas imported into and consumed in Singapore, across both piped natural gas and liquefied natural gas (LNG).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is critical because even though methane emitted directly from Singapore is low, the use of natural gas as a source of energy could indirectly contribute significantly to methane emissions through upstream fugitive emission leakages, if these are not properly controlled.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a responsible consumer of natural gas, be it piped or LNG, it is important that we uphold strict monitoring and verification standards and promote the adoption of emission reduction technologies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Having spoken much about the AR6 findings and their implications for Singapore, Mr Deputy Speaker, I do have a number of clarifications I would like to raise about the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To begin with, I note that the Bill under section 40A provides certain definitions on GHG goods, GHG works and other interpretations of the new Part 10A.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first clarification is about sections 40A and 40B which deal with the power of the Minister, after consultation with NEA, to prescribe any class, description or type of GHG goods to be regulated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To provide greater visibility to businesses and consumers, I would like to ask the Minister if there is currently a set of goods by which the Ministry and NEA plans to prescribe and regulate as GHG goods once the Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If there is not such a list yet, would the Minister and agency consider putting a plan for such a list such that, by the time the Act comes into force, the Government may facilitate a swift recognition of such goods?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How much of such goods and works that are available in our market today will now be subject to these amendments?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In addition, could the Minister provide clarity on whether these GHG goods or works were originally excluded from the Carbon Pricing Act and if so, what is the assessment of the cost to measure and report these GHG goods compared to the amount of carbon tax that potentially could be collected?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, I would like to ask the Minister what is the Ministry’s assessment of any possible impacts this amendment and the classification of the new GHG goods or works will have on our companies, such as the air-condition, chiller and equipment manufacturers as well as industries, such as the semiconductor manufacturing industry, which uses fluorinated gases?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Thirdly, under section 40D, there are proposed restrictions on supplies and imports of regulated goods.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To which, Minister Grace Fu shared that a review is ongoing and the decision for Singapore to ratify the Kigali Amendment will be finalised after consultation with key stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this Bill is but one of the many steps that Singapore will have to take in order for us to advance our efforts in addressing climate change.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As I shared in my speech on the Climate Motion earlier this year, even as a small island-state, Singapore has always been daring in our vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The science has spoken and there is no alternative except to urgently commit to reversing the trend of rising emissions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My fellow Sengkang colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, again had asked in a Parliamentary Question whether the Government plans to review Singapore's net zero emissions target and set a definitive timeline to achieve net zero emissions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Member Louis Ng too had asked in a Parliamentary Question whether the Government would review and bring forward the plans to reach net zero emissions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I ask that we be that bright green spark and show the world that even in spite of our constraints, we can set a bold, ambitious and specific emissions reductions target that aligns with the global goal of reaching net zero by 2050 and not let it be that because of our constraints, "if"s and "only if"s dominate our vocabulary.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Climate change is affecting every country in the world and Singapore is not spared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The IPCC report published last month is a sobering reminder of the disastrous outcomes we can expect in 2050 if planet-warming emissions, also known as Greenhouse Gases (GHGs), do not come down to net zero.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that the proposed amendments have balanced both the interests of businesses and protecting the environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, the methods to appeal against a Director-General's (DG) decision are not onerous, whereby aggrieved persons may simply apply to the DG by way of a written notice for reconsideration of the decision.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Ultimately, the objective of the Bill is to regulate GHG emissions in Singapore and this will eventually benefit all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I believe that these suggestions will allow for a more calibrated approach in ensuring that businesses comply with the amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, on the implementation of a register of suppliers, regulated goods and registered GHG entities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These provisions ensure that the Ministry retains oversight of all GHG goods and GHG-related stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is particularly valuable where GHG goods are subsequently found to have been falsely reported as conforming to prescribed standards.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The register will benefit suppliers of GHG goods in allowing them to recalibrate their business models where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Can we presume that similar to the prescribed regulated goods and suppliers under the Energy Conservation Act, that the register under the amendments will also be made available online?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Second, on the offences relating to the falsification of data in the proposed section 40X.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The falsification of data to the DG would render the objective of the Act nullified.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, suppliers would be able to supply GHG goods that blatantly fall afoul of the prescribed limits of emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, to ascertain the accuracy of every piece of information or data received would be operationally burdensome on the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have two suggestions for the Ministry's consideration.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Ministry impose a minimum fine for an offence under section 40X?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will encourage businesses to take extra effort to ensure the accuracy of information to be submitted to the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The said section prescribes that it is an offence to give false information to a public servant if one is legally bound to do so.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Lastly, I am concerned about the hardships SMEs and smaller businesses may face in complying with the amendments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Doing our part for climate change has a cost and the cost could be placed upon these SMEs unduly, especially in the short term.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the obligations under the proposed amendments will help to combat climate change, they will be especially onerous to smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, section 40D(4)(d) obligates suppliers of GHG goods to ensure that the goods are accompanied by information relating to their environmental impact.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: To this end, I have two suggestions to make.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While the impact of these obligations may not be large for individuals or larger businesses, I fear that SMEs may be adversely impacted in the short run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is worsened by the fact that some businesses may still be suffering from the effects of the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The new obligations imposed on related businesses are akin to new skillsets for their workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An appropriately timed transitionary period will allow businesses the required time to adequately comply with the new obligations and retrain their workers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Ministry can explore working with the unions and trade associations in providing practical information to affected SMEs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, while the definition of who qualifies as a competent person has yet to be published, the union stands ready to conduct training programmes to ensure affected SMEs can comply with this new obligation with ease.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Perhaps the Ministry can also consider making such training courses approved courses under the SkillsFuture scheme for jobseekers who wish to update their skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These amendments feature a judicious, multi-pronged approach in targeting a key driver of climate change.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every one of us, businesses and consumers alike, have an important role in creating a sustainable Singapore for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am confident that by passing the Bill, the House will further cement its commitment towards a greener future for Singapore.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the cost to society of producing an additional unit of the good includes not only the cost of factor inputs like labour and capital but also the harm the firm causes to the environment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The result is that in the absence of government intervention, there is an overproduction of such a good and its concomitant emission of greenhouse gases.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As policy tools to fight climate change, the setting of regulatory standards, which is a command-and-control measure, works to complement the introduction of carbon taxes, which is a price mechanism measure.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When is it optimal to use the setting of regulatory standards, which target quantities directly and when is it optimal to use prices to achieve the aim of limiting greenhouse gas emissions?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: When the compliance costs of limiting greenhouse gas emissions are fairly uniform across firms in the economy and the harm imposed on the rest of society rises sharply when the amount of greenhouse gas emissions crosses a certain threshold, it is optimal to set regulatory standards.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In practice, however, compliance costs might differ across industries and even across firms in the same industry.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: For example, newer firms might more readily take advantage of clean technology not available to older firms when the latter made their investment decisions.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: A policy question is whether older firms should be given more time and help in resources to make the transition to adopting clean technology so that there might be differential standards across firms temporarily.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In an environment with uncertainty about the cost of compliance due to new technological development, setting the same regulatory standard for all firms runs the risk of two possible types of error.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: If the actual cost of compliance turns out to be less than initially expected, then regulation would, in retrospect, have turned out to be too stringent.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, if the actual cost of compliance turns out to be higher than initially expected, then regulation would, in retrospect, have turned out to be too lax.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It might be preferable under uncertainty to set a tax on greenhouse gas emissions and then allow firms to choose the extent to which they wish to control the amount of emissions so it gives firms some buffer time to transit.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is, therefore, a basis for government intervention to limit the amount of greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In combination with subsidies for research and development in clean technology, this set of policy tools can steer Singapore in the direction of being a leader in sustainable living.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   I support the new regulations to reduce HFCs emitted by refrigeration and air-conditioning equipment.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentioned by my colleague Louis Ng, I share his concerns.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am concerned too with the details concerning certified technicians who handle refrigerants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of these employees are not very proficient in English.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What are the plans to help these workers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Government provide free training before the test?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will training be arranged on a regular basis to ensure that all technicians keep up with the technological changes in this sector?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Sir, not all job sites will be forbidden from carrying on with work during extended hours and on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have received quite a number of feedback regarding noise pollution from residents over the years, even though the construction sites producing the noise are some distance away.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a continued need to improve on the noise insulation properties of new and existing flats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I urge the Ministry to continue to look into the use of technology to minimise the noise pollution from construction projects.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Under most emissions scenarios that are being modelled today, the global surface temperature will most certainly continue to increase until the middle of this century.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In the coming years and decades, we will experience changes in our climate system with increase in heatwaves, droughts and more intense storms.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Here in Singapore, we will most probably experience heavier precipitation.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Throughout the world, we will continue to see the massive loss of sea ice, snow cover and permafrost.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many of such changes were caused by past greenhouse gas emissions and are irreversible for centuries and up to a millennia.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: These changes and impact are most prevalent in our ice sheets and global sea levels.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Today's emissions and the emissions of the future, will further contribute to these irreversible changes: ocean warming, ocean acidification, deoxygenation, melting glaciers and ice sheets, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Recently, I visited Pulau Ubin – lovely island.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The waves were crashing onto the sides of the rocks near the jetty.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It would probably take less than another metre of sea level rise before the seawater would flood the coastal roads.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must do more to better control and regulate our greenhouse emissions, be bold and quicken the pace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These measures, coupled with effective enforcement, will definitely go a long way to help mitigate climate change.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I have some concerns about the amendment to ensure that construction sites remain quiet on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the pandemic, many construction projects have been delayed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, with our economy gradually adjusting to a new norm, contractors are trying to catch up on the works in progress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With the shortage of workers and the urgency to rush jobs, more machinery might be used.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Then, what comes immediately to mind is safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So again, another delicate balance between productivity and safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Ministry be stepping up safety briefings and inspections?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the same CCTVs be used to enhance safety at the worksites?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The purpose is not so much to penalise and punish contractors, but rather to help spot any safety concerns early.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will allow contractors to be alerted and take remedial action to ensure safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I have a query about the integrity of the video recordings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I had encountered cases in my community where NEA received complaints from residents about noise but when they went down to check the construction sites, the noise level was considered acceptable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As technology is so advanced, how can we be sure that the recordings that both the residents and NEA encountered are similar?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The layman does not know what is an acceptable noise level and what is not.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These would be very helpful, so that residents are informed and can tell if rules have been flouted.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   I have some questions regarding the amendment to ensure that construction sites remain quiet on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Due to the pandemic, many construction projects had been delayed.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Now, many contractors are trying to expedite their works.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How are we going to balance their need to expedite construction, while at the same time, ensure that the noise pollution is maintained at an acceptable level?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, in this situation of rushing for work to be done, how do we ensure safety at worksites?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry will require errant contractors to install video surveillance systems.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we ensure that the recordings will not be tampered with?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Most residents do not know what the acceptable noise level is, as set by the Ministry.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My concern is that some of these measures will increase costs for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, low Global Warming Potential (GWP) commercial water-cooled chillers cost more upfront.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can also expect the higher costs to impact end-users.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What measures does the Government have to help manage the impact?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure that our cold chain needs will not be adversely affected by the increased costs?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another area contributing to higher costs is the certification of technicians handling refrigerants.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Only certified technicians will be permitted to supervise or service chillers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am concerned that such unnecessary costs will be levied on these SMEs and many of them are already suffering now.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, are the relevant departments considering using other measures to ensure that construction companies abide by the no-work regulations and better manage construction noise?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, what measures have the Ministry’s agencies implemented to reduce construction noise in residential areas?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can we use mobile phones to report errant contractors?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is pertinent in densely populated Singapore, where there are many concurrent ongoing construction activities, with some at close proximity to residential areas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially pronounced in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are construction works going on for the North-South Corridor and the new Thomson-East Coast Line.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: New BTO flats and private estate projects are being built in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are also existing upgrading works, for instance, at Mayflower Primary School.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I am happy to see such developments, many are taking place simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The effects of accumulated noise and dust can be vexing to residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, many projects have been extended due to COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have received many feedback on noise pollution at my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my speech, I will focus on managing noise from construction sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Over the years, authorities have increasingly leveraged on technology to monitor noise levels at construction sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, feedback from residents in the vicinity remains important, as they are personally impacted and may have practical concerns.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, there should be dedicated feedback channels for residents to relay their concerns to the contractor.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There should also be clear escalation protocols to NEA as the regulator, should problems remain unresolved, despite the initial feedback to the contractor.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be in the form of information on display boards, as well as flyers distributed to nearby blocks.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: NEA should also consider using Municipal Services Office (MSO)'s OneService app to push out notifications to residents living near construction sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will give ample time to residents, whether it is to facilitate alternative arrangements, or to find ways to mitigate the noise.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Contact details for the contractor and the relevant NEA feedback channels must also be clear and visible to residents.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On my rounds, I noticed that the display of contact details was not uniform for all sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some constructions sites display their contact details and project information on a large board.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, for certain works, especially smaller-scale ones, the information is not always immediately visible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some residents can therefore be surprised to see a barricaded project site appear, out of the blue.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They do not know what it was for and do not know who to ask.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Ministry can standardise the format and requirements for displaying relevant information and communication channels.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, there needs to be more public education with regards to no-work days.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Work is allowed on weekends for projects that meet certain criteria.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nevertheless, the ground reality is that this is not publicly known.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, members of public would lodge a complaint when they see construction works during the weekends, despite the works being permitted by NEA.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the COVID-19-related delays, I expect that more projects would seek permission to work on weekends.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, there needs to be more awareness and better understanding of the regulations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is to avoid wasting residents' time and Government's resources to manage redundant feedback.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we need to ensure that video surveillance support remains sustainable and effective.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One of the common reasons worksites contravene no-work days is because they are racing against a deadline and budget.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, my concern is if quality video surveillance equipment is costly to install and maintain, they may have some challenges setting it up within the stipulated timeline.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some errant contractors may even try to cut corners.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, as technology becomes increasingly sophisticated, we are observing a rise in digital capabilities to tamper with video equipment to create false content.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will NEA ensure that the equipment would not be tampered with, to present a fallacious impression?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides construction sites, I would like to seek clarification as to whether it also covers other projects that generate noise and other possible disruptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are small scale infrastructure developments in the housing estates like the building of covered linkways by the Town Council, piping works by PUB, or road works by LTA covered as well?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What about home renovations for HDB and condominium apartments, as well as additions and alterations for houses in landed estates?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The legislation ought to have a clearer definition on the projects it applies to.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be determined by the project scale or some other measurable criteria, such as the amount of noise pollution emitted or the number of residents that would be impacted.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Once the types of project sites are identified, we should also incrementally move towards having mandatory sound and dust-proof barriers for all these work sites.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many Singaporeans, Sundays and public holidays are the only days in a week when they can take a break and recharge.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Loud noise over prolonged periods triggers anxiety and stress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is exacerbated by work-from-home arrangements during this pandemic period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Also, noise monitoring should not be limited to volume alone, but also frequency.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Having mediated for community disputes among neighbours previously, some arising from construction noise, I can attest first-hand to the impact of unwanted noise on one’s mental well-being.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also require such offences to be highlighted, when they next bid for projects.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Issues relating to construction noise have been consistently brought up in Parliament on several occasions over the past 10 years, despite ongoing reviews to manage disamenities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Instead of having discrete and piecemeal recommendations, we need a multifaceted and holistic approach to tackle noise pollution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As mentioned in my speech, these include better feedback management, promoting greater public awareness of no-work days and having stronger guidelines on surveillance systems.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should also have greater clarity on the type of construction projects covered under the new amendments and have more enforcement bite.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I believe that these suggestions working together as a system, will make a difference on the ground.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The thoughtful comments and suggestions that were raised reflect our collective commitment to climate action and to provide a quality living environment for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I will first address Members’ questions on the measures to reduce HFC emissions from refrigeration and air-conditioning, or RAC, equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: HFC accounts for a sizeable share of Singapore’s greenhouse gas emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As Mr Louis Ng pointed out, there was a 30% increase in HFC emissions from 2014 to 2016 and this underscores the urgent need for action, which Mr Shawn Huang as well as Mr Louis Chua have also emphasised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The measures introduced today will deliver deep cuts in HFC emissions and bring us closer to our climate goals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Companies can continue to use their existing equipment until the end of life for those equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While low-GWP chillers may cost a little more, they are typically more energy and carbon efficient and offer net cost savings over their lifecycle.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, investing in them not only protects the climate, but also protects companies from being locked into the higher operating costs of less efficient chillers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Companies that are replacing their chillers in the immediate future can tap on the grant introduced in October 2020 to incentivise the early switch to low-GWP chillers, before the supply restriction comes into force in October 2022.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: One grant recipient is Kaer Pte Ltd, an energy services company which provides "Cooling as a Service".

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: With grant support, Kaer is replacing chillers at an industrial facility with climate-friendly ones that not only use low-GWP refrigerant, but will also improve the system’s energy efficiency by 35%.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As Mr Louis Ng has highlighted, proper refrigerant handling practices are important to minimise HFC emissions during servicing and maintenance of RAC equipment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We have worked closely with Temasek Polytechnic and industry partners to develop a training and certification programme for chiller technicians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This two-day programme has been designed to be practical and relevant to the industry and will cover the processes for handling and recovering refrigerants from chillers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Technicians will be re-certified every three years to keep up with advancements in technology.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked whether the course could be held in other languages aside from English.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The course is designed to meet the needs of the technicians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It will be conducted in simple spoken English.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Temasek Polytechnic has ample experience in conducting other similar technical courses and trainers will tailor their delivery to suit the language competency of the technicians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Trainers will also give practical demonstrations and conduct hands-on practice to enhance understanding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: To be certified, technicians have to pass an open-book test comprising multiple choice questions and a simple practical assessment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In fact, during my visit to Temasek Polytechnic, I noticed that the course will be conducted, hands-on, by technicians for the technicians themselves.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, it will be done in a simple manner, using languages that the technicians can understand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Desmond Choo, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have asked if there would be financial support for these technicians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We agree with Mr Desmond Choo that companies need time to develop internal processes and train their technicians.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: For this reason, we announced the requirements early in March last year.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We have since been engaging the industry closely to develop these measures and will continue to do so to ensure a smooth transition.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I am also pleased to inform Mr Desmond Choo that the register for registered suppliers and registered regulated goods will be made accessible online.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This was a question that was asked by Mr Louis Chua as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Desmond Choo also proposed stricter penalties for the offence of falsifying information or data under the new section 40X.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The penalty of a fine not exceeding $5,000 or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or both, is aligned to similar offences under the Energy Conservation Act.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: From our experience, this serves as sufficient deterrence and we will review the penalty level should data falsification become an issue of concern, going forward.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Don Wee asked whether requiring spent refrigerants to be recovered and treated will add to business cost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This is unlikely, as most of the spent refrigerants can be treated for reuse and have commercial value.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Today, even in the absence of regulation, there is already a market for them and facilities to treat spent refrigerants are already available.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked about our plans to address HFC emissions beyond the current measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We are studying the potential for other types of RAC equipment, such as commercial and industrial refrigeration units, to switch to low-GWP refrigerants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We will need to assess the feasibility of available technologies, balancing considerations such as fire safety, toxicity, energy efficiency and the cost of suitable substitutes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In response to Mr Louis Chua, we will consult and work closely with industries and businesses, and give sufficient lead time before implementing any measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I assure Mr Don Wee that we will carefully consider the cost impact on our cold chain needs when assessing any future measures on commercial and industrial refrigeration units.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The measures introduced today have no impact on cold chain needs, as climate-friendly household refrigerators do not cost more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Prof Hoon Hian Teck asked whether it would be better to price HFC emissions rather than regulate these.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While pricing remains an option, there are merits in adopting regulations to reduce HFC emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: HFC emissions arise mainly from ownership rather than the intensity of use of RAC equipment and are locked in by technology choices.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Given technical complexity and the need to balance multiple considerations in the choice of refrigerants as highlighted earlier, it is difficult for end-users to make informed choices or to influence upstream supplier decisions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Regulation offers much greater outcome certainty in abating HFC emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: In commercial chillers, for example, regulation will effect a switch to a new generation of refrigerants with GWP close to zero, bringing HFC emissions to negligible levels when the entire stock of chillers turns over.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Even if taxation were to be introduced, these considerations mean that regulations may still be needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We would have to consider the cost effectiveness of the taxation regime, given the highly distributed sources of emissions.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While the tax can be levied upstream on importers, this has to be coupled with the system of downstream rebates for spent refrigerants that are recovered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This could potentially result in higher administrative costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Louis Chua also asked about the abatement potential and plans for the Kigali Amendment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I will now address Members’ questions on construction noise and the requirement for contractors, who have violated the no-work rule, to install, maintain and operate video surveillance at their construction sites.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: First, let me address questions on the implementation of the requirement for video surveillance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked about the types of construction projects that are covered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The current regulations state that all construction sites located less than 150 metres from any hospital, home for the aged sick or residential building must comply with the no-work rule on Sundays and public holidays.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The Bill does not change the no-work rule regulation or requirement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Under this Bill, the Director-General may now impose the requirement for video surveillance on any construction site that contravenes the no-work rule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: So, the site has to contravene the rule first.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The requirement applies to all public and private sector construction projects, regardless of the size, if they violate the no-work rule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It is important to ensure the integrity and proper functioning of the video surveillance systems, as Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Joan Pereira have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: NEA will carry out scheduled and surprise site inspections to ensure that the video surveillance systems are in good working condition and not tampered with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The new section 28A empowers the Director-General to specify requirements for the video surveillance system, including ensuring that the system's security is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: For example, contractors should implement robust digital identification (ID) and password controls and restrict access to the physical components of the system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The person required to install, to operate and to maintain the video surveillance system under the new section 28A must also take all reasonable steps to ensure that no person tampers with or does anything to compromise the proper functioning of the system or any image, sound or video recorded by the system.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Don Wee asked whether phone video footages can be used to substantiate complaints on no-work rule violations in place of video surveillance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: While phone video footages can be used as evidence for prosecution, they might not capture sufficient information on the construction activities being carried out to conclude that there was indeed an offence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Such footages received from the public might also not be timely enough to address ongoing construction noise infringements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: On the other hand, the installed video surveillance will allow NEA to remotely monitor construction worksites and deter repeat violations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It enhances NEA's efficiency and responsiveness, removing the need for officers to carry out repeated inspections to address recurring public feedback.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: I assure Mr Don Wee and Mr Yip Hon Weng that we are mindful of the impact of the measures on the construction industry, which is facing challenging times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: It will not affect the vast majority of construction sites that comply with the no-work rule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng highlighted other complementary measures to strengthen compliance to the no-work rule, such as introducing higher penalties.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The vast majority of construction sites comply with the no-work rule.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: NEA will monitor the effectiveness of these measures in this Bill to address the remaining small group of non-compliant contractors and consider further measures, if needed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We have to strike a careful balance between maintaining a conducive living environment and also allowing construction work to be completed within a reasonable duration and cost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We need to maintain a steady supply of public housing, continue expanding our public transport network and provide amenities such as hospitals and schools.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: As Mr Yip Hon Weng pointed out, many projects have been significantly delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This impacts end users such as families waiting to move into their Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Project delays not only affect the construction industry and end users, they also prolong the disamenities experienced by neighbouring residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Ms Joan Pereira also spoke about balancing the need to expedite projects that have been delayed while keeping disamenities to acceptable levels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: This, in fact, is the balance that we need to strike.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for an update on the review of construction noise limits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We recognise that the construction sector faces serious manpower and supply shortages during these extraordinary times.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng gave useful suggestions to improve feedback management for residents, including having dedicated feedback channels, clear escalation protocols, standardising format for displaying communication channels and providing advance notice to residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Many of these measures are already in place and we will see how to improve and enhance them.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: For example, as part of construction works that require a BCA permit, the contractor must erect a project signboard of at least 1.8 metres in width and one metre in height before work can commence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The project signboard displays information of the project parties and their contact numbers as well as the hotline numbers of MOM, NEA and BCA.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Residents can also submit their feedback through the NEA website and the myENV and OneService mobile applications.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Upon receiving feedback, NEA officers will investigate whether the construction site has generated noise levels exceeding the noise limits or violated the no-work rule and then, they take enforcement actions accordingly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: NEA has also been advising contractors to engage the nearby residents early to develop plans to minimise the impact of construction work on residents' daily lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Contractors have also been encouraged to implement additional noise mitigation measures where possible, such as noise barriers for noisy works like hacking and drilling.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We acknowledge Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms Joan Pereira's suggestions on improving the public's awareness of the rules on construction noise.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Information on construction noise limits, permissible work hours and the no-work rule is published on NEA's website.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Members of the public can reach out to NEA through various communication channels to find out if a particular construction site is permitted to carry out quieter works on Sunday and public holidays or if noise limits have been breached.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: NEA will explore raising public awareness on the no-work rule via social media channels.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: On Mr Gan Thiam Poh's suggestion to improve the noise-insulating properties of HDB flats, HDB will continue to explore practical noise mitigation measures for the comfort and well-being of residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Given our high-density environment and with HDB flats being designed for natural ventilation, some noise will inevitably make its way into flats through our open windows and doors.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We will continue to work with stakeholders to better manage construction noise in order to maintain a conducive living environment while allowing projects to keep pace with providing infrastructure and amenities for our residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: The early switch to low-GWP equipment and proper management of HFC refrigerants will ensure that the cooling needs and comfort of Singaporeans will not be compromised as we transit to a low-carbon future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: Imposing electronic video surveillance on construction sites which have violated the no-work rule is an important step and addition to our existing enforcement measures.

speaker: Mr Desmond Tan
text: We hope this requirement will improve compliance and help NEA to manage public feedback more effectively.
